studies.title: OFC-induced network modularity improves positive symptoms and attentional alertness in schizophrenia: a combined rTMS-fMRI study
studies.abstract: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 4 weeks of low-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) targeting the right orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) in first-episode schizophrenia. Combined rTMS-fMRI analysis showed that modularization between the OFC and the default mode network (DMN) across time windows supported improvements in positive symptoms and attentional alertness. rTMS targeting the OFC improves attentional vigilance and positive symptoms in drug-naïve patients with first-episode schizophrenia, potentially via OFC-DMN network modularity changes.

studies.title: The efficacy of transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) combined with cognitive behavioural therapy for major depressive disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
studies.abstract: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials evaluating the efficacy of tDCS combined with cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) versus sham tDCS plus CBT for major depressive disorder (MDD). Included 5 RCTs with 173 patients. The combination of tDCS and CBT did not demonstrate a significant additional benefit compared with sham tDCS plus CBT for MDD. Despite the theoretical hypothesis that tDCS may enhance cognitive control to synergize with CBT, current RCT evidence does not support incremental benefit of active tDCS over sham when combined with CBT.

studies.title: Noninvasive brain stimulation combined with evidence-based psychotherapy for psychiatric disorders: A meta-analysis of optimal implementation parameters
studies.authors: Beynel L, Wiener E, Baker N, Greenstein E, Neacsiu AD, Jones E, Gindoff B, Francis SM, Neige C, Mondino M, Davis SW, Luber B, Lisanby SH, Deng ZD
studies.abstract: Meta-analysis following Cochrane methods, searching 6 databases through February 2025, screening 1,017 records. Examined whether combining noninvasive brain stimulation (NIBS — rTMS or tDCS) with evidence-based psychotherapy (EBP) improves outcomes compared with sham NIBS plus psychotherapy across psychiatric disorders. Key findings: rTMS (but not tDCS) was significantly effective when combined with psychotherapy; non-concurrent delivery (stimulation and psychotherapy delivered in separate sessions) was superior to concurrent delivery; significant effects were found only for anxiety disorders but not depression or other conditions. The study identifies critical parameters for optimising combined NIBS-psychotherapy protocols.

studies.title: A systematic review of transcranial magnetic stimulation for generalized anxiety disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and posttraumatic stress disorder
studies.abstract: Systematic review of RCTs evaluating transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) for generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Searched PubMed, Cochrane Library and PsycINFO for English-language studies published through July 7, 2025, identifying 20 RCTs evaluating efficacy and 18 RCTs evaluating safety. For remission, no evidence of benefit for TMS compared with sham was found for any condition. However, active TMS produced greater clinical response for OCD compared to sham. TMS probably improves clinical response in OCD and may improve symptom severity in GAD, OCD, and PTSD. Further research is recommended to determine optimal brain targets and treatment parameters.

studies.title: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation: advances for psychiatric disorders
studies.authors: Wu Z, Xu Y, Huang Q, Liu B, Zhou S
studies.abstract: Narrative review from Dalian Medical University discussing advances in rTMS for major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and generalized anxiety disorder. Clinical efficacy of rTMS is highly dependent on the precise matching of stimulation parameters (frequency, intensity, total number of pulses, treatment course) with target brain regions (dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, supplementary motor area, temporal-parietal cortex). The review summarises current evidence and research directions.

studies.title: rTMS for treatment resistant depression - a single center community experience
studies.authors: Jacques FH, Godin C, Rabia N, Apedaile BE
studies.abstract: Retrospective chart review of patients with treatment-resistant depression (TRD) treated with rTMS at a Canadian community clinic (Clinic Neuro-Outaouais Gatineau) over ten years (2015-2025) using sequential bilateral hemisphere stimulation. Reviewed real-world effectiveness including response and remission rates and long-term follow-up outcomes. The study documents community-based experience with rTMS for TRD outside of academic clinical trials.

studies.title: Non-Invasive Brain Stimulation in Older Inpatients with Depression: A Real-World Comparison of Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) and Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation (tDCS) on Depressive Symptoms and Functional Recovery
studies.abstract: Retrospective, naturalistic comparative study of 104 depressed inpatients aged 60 years or older (unipolar or bipolar), treated with either rTMS (n=48) or tDCS (n=56) as part of routine clinical care at Vita-Salute San Raffaele University, Milan, Italy. Depression severity assessed with 21-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HDRS21) at baseline, 2 weeks, and 1 month; functional outcomes assessed with Global Assessment of Functioning (GAF) at admission and discharge. At 1 month, response and remission rates were significantly higher in the rTMS group compared to the tDCS group; GAF improvement was comparable between the two groups.

studies.title: Transcranial direct current stimulation combined with cognitive-behavioral interventions for depressive disorders: a systematic review and meta-analysis of sham-controlled randomized trials
studies.authors: Da Silva OAFS, Pereira SIDS, et al.
studies.abstract: Systematic review and meta-analysis of sham-controlled randomized trials examining the combination of tDCS with cognitive-behavioral interventions (CBIs) for depressive disorders. Current evidence does not demonstrate a reliable incremental benefit of adjunctive tDCS over sham when paired with heterogeneous CBIs in patients with depressive disorders. Findings should be interpreted with caution because of methodological heterogeneity in intervention parameters and insufficient statistical power.
